options.text: The administration first froze and capped prices, then removed the caps while shortages continued

options.misconception: Dates the end of controls to the late 1970s

questions.explanation: The 1971 freeze and the phased program that followed capped prices and wages, and the caps came off by 1974 while shortages and rising costs persisted. Inflation continued for other reasons.
questions.hint: Look for the sequence of freeze, caps, and removal.

questions.stem: The translator's note for the 1974 legal history chapter asks you to reconcile two statements: the decision was legally binding, and the practice it ordered went on unchanged for a decade.

options.text: Both hold: courts set the rule, but implementation needed follow-up decisions, funding, and political will
Only the first statement holds, because the second misstates what courts can do

options.misconception: Denies the legal force of judicial decisions

options.text: Neither holds, because practice never changed until the ruling was overturned

questions.explanation: A court states a rule; other institutions carry it out. Follow-up rulings, budget authority, and political will shape enforcement, so a binding decision can coexist with unchanged practice.

options.misconception: Treats referenda as a lawful veto mechanism

answer.exemplar: Congress had added a temporary surcharge on income taxes in 1968 to cool an overheated economy, and the 1971 revenue act repealed it while cutting individual rate schedules. questions.explanation: The 1971 act repealed the surcharge and lowered rate schedules, easing the bracket-creep squeeze on middle-income households, but the resulting demand supported prices that were already climbing.

questions.stem: Translator's note 61 for the education appendix asks you to explain, for readers, how the first big federal school aid program of the era identified the children it was meant to help.

answer.exemplar: Title I of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 directed money to school districts with large numbers of children from low-income families, and the money was meant for programs such as reading help, counseling, and materials rather than for building budgets in general. The act also funded other titles, including library services and equipment, and state agencies administered the program. questions.topic: A ruling left unenforced
questions.learningObjective: Explain why desegregation decisions went unenforced for years
questions.stem: Translator's note 73 for the civil rights chapter asks you to explain, for the timeline, why the 1954 decision produced almost no integrated classrooms for the better part of a decade.

answer.exemplar: The 1954 decision declared state school segregation unconstitutional, but it did not say how quickly schools had to comply, and the 1968 follow-up permitted desegregation at a pace local courts judged reasonable. Southern officials resisted, state legislatures passed laws meant to block implementation, and the federal government, which had only recently begun to press for compliance, lacked the machinery to force dozens of districts at once. Court orders backed by federal pressure produced the change that had not come from the decision alone.

questions.explanation: The delay came from a vague remedy, official resistance, and slow federal enforcement. Courts needed years of follow-up rulings and federal pressure to turn principle into practice.
questions.hint: Look at the remedy and the resistance to it.

questions.stem: Translator's note 44 for the welfare file asks you to describe, for the appendix, what a family had to do and prove to keep receiving cash assistance in the 1970s.

answer.exemplar: Cash assistance for families with dependent children was run by the states within federal rules that counted income and resources, set a state maximum, and required recipients to accept work, training, or schooling when able to do so. Mothers were often pushed into work placements, and payments were set below the amount local wage standards assumed a family needed. The program therefore functioned as conditional aid rather than a simple income floor, and many recipients left the rolls once their circumstances changed or their cases were reviewed.

questions.explanation: Eligibility rested on federal rules for income and resources, and the aid carried work or training conditions. That conditional design distinguished it from an unconditional payment.

answer.exemplar: Civil rights lawyers argued that equal citizenship required more than a formal right to attend school: children in poor districts needed teachers, books, and buildings that a wealthy district took for granted, and the schools built after 1954 often re-segregated students by ability and by housing patterns. questions.stem: Translator's note 78 for the fiscal history asks you to explain, for readers, why a tax system written for stable prices produced unpleasant surprises in the 1970s.

answer.exemplar: The income tax was written as a schedule of rates applied to brackets of income measured in dollars, and the bracket boundaries were only occasionally adjusted for inflation. When wages rose because prices rose, households crossed a bracket boundary without becoming richer in any real sense, and their tax bill grew. The same wage gains also pushed workers into higher rates through payroll deductions. Only later in the decade did indexing of the thresholds begin to hold the tax system steady, and the earlier years left a record of families paying more tax on less real income.

questions.explanation: Unindexed brackets turned inflation-driven raises into higher liabilities, and payroll tax rates added to the load, so real after-tax income fell even as paychecks grew. Indexing arrived only later.
questions.hint: Think about a schedule written in dollars, not real terms.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: One national standard for air and water
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the effect of a uniform rule on local practice

stimulus.body: The mill has begun installing the equipment the federal permit requires, even though the county has never written a rule of its own. Officials in the neighbouring county, where nothing has been required yet, say the same rule will reach them before long, and the mill expects the same cost for everyone.

questions.stem: Note 32 for the press clippings file asks what the dispatch shows about the reach of the national standard.

options.text: A uniform federal rule changed practice in a county whose state had done little, since it applied everywhere
The mill built the equipment because the county adopted its own strict permit first
options.misconception: Credits a local rule for the mill's investment

options.text: The dispatch shows that federal permits applied only in states that requested them
options.misconception: Makes the national program optional by state request

options.text: The mill delayed the work until neighbouring counties had installed the same equipment
options.misconception: Reverses the sequence of investments

questions.explanation: The dispatch shows the federal rule reaching a county without local rules, since the standard applied nationwide. No local adoption or state request produced the change.
questions.hint: Look for the rule that applied without a local counterpart.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A benefit a family could claim
questions.learningObjective: Reconcile the reasons for growth in benefit participation
questions.stem: Note 46 for the social survey asks you to reconcile two explanations for the growth in food stamp participation: more counties offered the program, and the benefit grew more generous.

options.text: Both contributed: wider availability and larger benefits together explain the growth in households served
Only availability explains it, because benefit amounts were fixed in nominal terms throughout
options.misconception: Denies any change in benefit generosity

options.text: Only generosity explains it, because the program was already offered in every county
options.misconception: Overstates the program's coverage of counties

options.text: Neither explains it, because participation was flat through the decade
options.misconception: Denies the recorded growth in participation

questions.explanation: Participation rose because the program became available in more counties while benefit amounts grew with the cost of living, so reach and generosity worked together. Neither alone explains it.
questions.hint: Weigh reach against the size of the benefit.
